title: Iran to impose restricted shipping zone near Strait of Hormuz
summary:
Iran to impose restricted shipping zone near Strait of Hormuz

Iran plans to establish a restricted maritime zone near the Strait of Hormuz within days, state media has quoted the country’s top security official as saying.

The designated area will stretch from the boundary of the US naval blockade into parts of the Gulf. Tehran will place any vessel that enters the zone on its sanctions list, the official said.

Iran and Oman also expect to sign new maps regulating maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz in the coming days, according to Iranian state television.

title: Germany's far-right, pro-Israel AfD sweeps Saxony-Anhalt in historic electoral breakthrough
summary:
Germany's far-right, pro-Israel AfD sweeps Saxony-Anhalt in historic electoral breakthrough

Submitted by MEE staff on Sun, 09/06/2026 - 19:40
The AfD's historic breakthrough in the Germany state cements a party that courts Israel while building its platform on anti-Muslim and anti-Palestine politics
The co-leader of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party Alice Weidel gives an interview as she arrives at the AfD's election party following Saxony-Anhalt's state elections in Magdeburg, eastern Germany on September 6, 2026. (Ronny Hartmann/AFP)
Off

Germany’s far-right and avowedly pro-Israel Alternative for Germany (AfD) has swept the state election in Saxony-Anhalt, bringing the party within reach of governing a German state for the first time since the end of the Nazi period.

The AfD secured 44.5 percent of the vote, according to an ARD exit poll, more than doubling its 2021 share. Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union trailed far behind on 18.5 percent.

Reuters reported turnout of about 76 percent, significantly higher than is typical for German state elections.

"We have made history in this country," Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s 35-year-old lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, said speaking to Reuters.

It remains unclear whether the AfD can secure enough seats or find the political support needed to form a state government.

The result has already set off alarm bells in France. Jean-Luc Melenchon, one of the country’s leading opposition politicians, warned on X that “The far right is back in Germany”.

Calling the result a “disaster”, Melenchon added that “under these conditions, the German military project to create Europe's first conventional army is unacceptable for France.”

German court rules comparing Israel to Nazi Germany constitutes 'protected speech'
Read More »

The AfD’s classification as a far-right party has not stopped members of Israel’s government from considering it a potential political partner.

In February 2025, Israeli Diaspora Affairs Minister Amichai Chikli praised the anti-Islam and anti-Palestinian party for targeting groups that campaign for Palestinian rights.

Chikli said that, “surprisingly”, the AfD had led efforts to challenge German support for organisations critical of Israel.

“It was also the AfD that initiated a bill in April 2019 calling for a ban on the antisemitic BDS movement… In June 2019, the AfD also proposed a complete ban on Hezbollah’s activities in Germany,” wrote Chikli in a post on X at the time.

The AfD leadership has sought to present the party as an unflinching supporter of Israel despite repeated antisemitic and Holocaust-revisionist statements from figures within its ranks.

During a conversation with Elon Musk in January 2025, AfD co-leader Alice Weidel described her party as “the only protector of the Jewish people” in Germany.

Weidel has tied the AfD’s support for Israel directly to its campaigns against Muslims and immigration, casting the Israeli state as a partner in the party’s wider confrontation with Islam and Muslims.

title: Balkans: Israel deepens ties with Bosnian Serb separatists through Banja Luka trade office

Balkans: Israel deepens ties with Bosnian Serb separatists through Banja Luka trade office

Israeli officials opened an Israeli Chamber of Commerce office on Thursday in Banja Luka, the seat of Republika Srpska.

The nationalist leadership of the Serb-dominated entity has pursued an increasingly separatist agenda threatening Bosnia and Herzegovina’s unity while fostering closer relations with Israel.

The opening of the Chamber of Commerce marks another step in Israel’s push for greater influence in the Balkans as it faces increasing international isolation.

It also reflects Israel’s growing willingness to cultivate destabilising political movements and entities seeking greater autonomy or independence from internationally recognised states.

The higly controversial Israeli Diaspora Minister Amichai Chikli attended the ceremony. Chikli has supported the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians from Gaza.

title: Using a VM to Contain an AI Agent
summary:
It won’t work:

My suspicion was that GPT 5.6-Cyber would succeed, but the frequency and manner of its success removed all doubt. We have to reassess sandboxing quality for capable AI agents, and in general the software stack with which they interact.

An off-the-shelf VM is not enough to contain a modern, cyber-capable AI agent. There is simply too much attack surface. Even innocuous features (like running with a display) add extra, exploitable attack surface.

title: Security Vulnerability in a Voting System
summary:
It’s a vulnerability that allows someone to recover the order of ballots cast, newly exploited with AI tools.

Nearly four years since the original vulnerability was disclosed, I was still able to use it to analyze voter behavior in Georgia (one of the 21 states that uses affected scanners) in the recent May 2026 primary.

Notably, I never touched a voting machine, exploited a network, examined source code, or accessed anything non-public.

After pointing a coding agent to the original vulnerability paper, I supplied it with two data sources highlighted in the paper: the early-voting list for each county, and the “CVR” (cast-vote record) file, containing every ballot and its selections (but not the voters’ names or other identifying information). The CVR file is available upon request, precisely because a public, ballot-level record is what makes election results independently verifiable...

title: AI Coding Agents Are Installing Unknown/Untrusted Code on Corporate Networks
summary:
We cannot forget that AI coding agents are not yet trustworthy:

Researchers at a stealth startup in Israel scanned 6,214 live domains belonging to defense contractors, Fortune 500, and Big Tech companies. Of the 8,265 llms.txt and llms-full.txt files they found (many sites hosted both an llms.txt and an llms-full.txt file), 120 of them, each on a different site, pointed to one or more code packages or domain names that weren’t registered. To test what happens when an AI agent processes such files, the researchers registered a handful of the unclaimed names and hosted packages that caused any machine executing them to reach out to their server. Within an hour, the researchers received a phone-home response from a Fortune 500 company. Over time, they got a few dozen more, some from more Fortune 500 companies and others from startups. Their beacon also recorded the chain of parent processes that spawned each install, ultimately revealing that coding agents, including Claude, OpenAI’s Codex, and Nous Research’s Hermes, were involved. Anthropic, OpenAI, and Nous Research did not respond to requests for comment by the time of publication...

title: Death toll from Israeli attacks on Lebanon climbs to 4,362 despite ceasefire
summary:
Death toll from Israeli attacks on Lebanon climbs to 4,362 despite ceasefire

Lebanon’s Health Ministry says Israel has killed 4,362 people and wounded 12,378 in attacks across the country since 2 March.

Israel has continued bombing Lebanon and occupying parts of its territory despite a ceasefire that took effect on 17 April and was renewed on 26 June.

Before the truce, Israeli troops seized nearly 2,000sq km (770sq miles), equivalent to about one-fifth of Lebanon. A buffer zone still covers approximately six percent of the country.

title: The world is finally watching Palestine. But who gets to narrate its story?
summary:
The world is finally watching Palestine. But who gets to narrate its story?

Submitted by Nour A Munawar on Sun, 09/06/2026 - 12:56
As courts and sports stadiums turn towards Palestine, a quieter struggle runs beneath the headlines over memory, heritage and the right of Palestinians to speak for themselves
A demonstrator waves a Palestinian flag as protesters march towards the Azteca Stadium during the opening of the World Cup in Mexico City on 11 June 2026 (Carlos Tischler/Eyepix Group via Reuters)
Off

Palestine did not qualify for this summer's Football World Cup. It hardly needed to. Activists opened the tournament by forming a human Palestinian flag in Mexico City, and at the Egypt-Iran match in Seattle, Palestinian flags flew behind the goals while chanting for Gaza.

When Bosnia and Herzegovina, a nation that survived its own genocide, reached the knockout rounds, its supporters filled stadiums with choruses of "Free Palestine" for a people enduring another.

Palestine had no team on the pitch, yet became one of the tournament's defining presences. In the past three years, the Palestinian flag has emerged not only as a symbol denouncing Israeli genocide, but as a global gesture against victimisation, injustice and colonial oppression.

The tournament ended in July, with Palestine emerging as its true winner. 

That visibility now comes with a measure of accountability. Last September, a UN commission of inquiry concluded that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza, where the health ministry has recorded more than 73,000 dead, around half of them women and children. Some 2,700 families have been wiped from the civil register.

The world's highest court is weighing a genocide case brought by South Africa and joined by more than a dozen states.

The International Criminal Court, meanwhile, has issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity, including starvation as a method of warfare.

Likewise, Palestine's growing visibility and support are reflected in global public opinion. Gallup found in February that, for the first time in a quarter-century of its polling, more Americans sympathise with Palestinians than with Israelis, while majorities in most of the 36 countries surveyed by Pew this spring view Israel negatively.

And yet, simultaneously, Palestinians are being exterminated; their homes and hospitals, schools, archives and universities are being destroyed - and with them the means to tell their own story.

This is the paradox of Palestine in a polarised world: never so widely seen, and never so thoroughly written about by others. The question is no longer only whether Palestine will be free, but who will have the permission and power to narrate it.

War on memory

Israel's destruction of Palestinian life has never been only physical. It has always carried a second purpose: to erase and unmake Palestinian memory.

As Munawar has argued elsewhere, the erasure of Palestinian heritage did not begin with this war. It reaches back to the 1948 Nakba and the villages emptied and renamed: an ongoing Nakba that Palestinian and Arab communities have long met with grassroots efforts to safeguard what state power seeks to erase.

By March 2026, Unesco had verified damage to 164 cultural sites in Gaza - mosques, churches, museums and archives - though Palestinian officials put the true figure far higher. UN experts recorded the destruction of all 12 of Gaza's universities and the burning of the Central Archives of Gaza, and questioned whether it amounted to "scholasticide".

To burn a people's archives and raze their universities is not incidental to a genocide; it is central to their annihilation

The assault also targets those documenting it: more than 200 Palestinian journalists have been killed since October 2023, while the Committee to Protect Journalists says the Israeli military has carried out more targeted killings of the press than any other government's military on record. Foreign reporters, meanwhile, remain barred from Gaza.

Even the dead are not spared: Israeli forces have bulldozed and desecrated at least 16 of Gaza's cemeteries, unearthing bodies as they advanced. The UN's genocide commission likewise counted attacks on cultural and religious sites among the acts that constitute war crimes.

To burn a people's archives and raze their universities is not incidental to a genocide; it is central to their annihilation. In Gaza, that strategy has reached its most total form as an attack not only on the living and the dead, but on a people's capacity to speak for itself.

This is why Palestine has become the sharpest test of a term western universities use freely, often carelessly: "Decolonisation." As Munawar has argued, decolonising heritage means more than revising a syllabus or a reading list.

It requires redistributing the power to decide what is preserved, restored and remembered, and who does the remembering. No case makes that argument more starkly than Palestine's.

Competing narratives

The question of who does the remembering was central to the 12th annual conference of the Amsterdam School for Heritage, Memory and Material Culture, which we convened at the University of Amsterdam this June. Participants asked what decolonial thinking has disrupted, dismantled and dreamt anew - and whether those gains can hold as resurgent nationalisms press back.

One of the conference's two keynote panels, "Decoloniality in Palestine: Law and Narrative Sovereignty", brought together the international crimes scholar Alette Smeulers, the Genocide Convention specialist Marieke de Hoon and the Palestinian theologian Mitri Raheb, author of Decolonizing Palestine: The Land, The People, The Bible.

The panel proceeded from the premise that international law functions in Palestine not as a neutral arbiter but as another site of struggle. It also examined how the religious and cultural narratives of Christian Zionism, long used to justify dispossession, are themselves ripe for unsettling. Panellists challenged Europe's selective invocation of international law: quick to cite against adversaries, slow against allies.

What the conference kept returning to was a discomfort closer to home. For decades, western institutions have lent their authority to Palestinian erasure, too often treating Israeli accounts as taken-for-granted facts while dismissing Palestinian accounts as untrustworthy opinions, recasting a colonised people's dispossession as a quarrel between equals.

Panels on contested memories and competing narratives asked what it means for scholars, especially Arab and Palestinian scholars working in the West, to refuse that reflex and restore Palestinians as authors of their own knowledge.

That refusal is visible inside the lecture hall and beyond. From Columbia to Amsterdam, students have held protests and encampments demanding that their universities reckon honestly with the genocide.

The school has also launched a new book series, "Palestine: Past, Present and Future Narratives", edited by one of us (Saloul) and devoted to countering "Eurocentric, orientalist traditions and hegemonic modes of knowledge production" about Palestine.

For a place so relentlessly described by outsiders, no task matters more than reconstituting Palestinian authorship. Set against the scale of the loss, this is a modest instrument. But narrative sovereignty is built from exactly such work: the patient work of ensuring Palestinians speak in their own voice and are heard.

Rebuilding over the rubble

The question of authorship now hangs over Gaza's reconstruction. The so-called "Board of Peace", devised and chaired by Donald Trump with no Palestinian representation on its executive tier, has pledged billions and delivered almost nothing.

Meanwhile, glossy renderings of a "New Gaza" of towers and marinas circulate as if Gaza were a blank coast awaiting investors.

The consequences of that hierarchy have only become clearer since Hamas dissolved the committee through which it governed Gaza in July, passing day-to-day administration to a technocratic body that answers, ultimately, to the board.

Israel has even rejected the logo of that Palestinian committee because it resembles the Palestinian Authority's emblem. Not even the symbols of Palestinian administration escape the veto.

Archiving Gaza in the present: The quest to preserve Palestinian memory
Read More »

Gaza is not a blank coast. To rebuild a place while killing the people to whom it belongs, and erasing what stood there before, is not recovery; it is ethnic cleansing by other means.

The region has been here before, and its rebuilt monuments offer both models and warnings.

Mostar's restored bridge and Mosul's al-Nuri mosque - rising again on its residents' terms - showed how reconstruction can support communal recovery. At Palmyra, by contrast, restoration was stage-managed into a spectacle of political power.

Rebuilding is always an argument over who owns the past, and it heals only when led by the people whose past it is.

In Gaza, narrative sovereignty has a concrete form: Palestinian-led reconstruction and heritage governance rather than a Palestinian-free board, the rescue and digitisation of archives, and communities deciding what is restored, what is memorialised and what is left standing as witness to Palestinian identity.

That work has begun in fragments, with Unesco mobilising $5.7m to stabilise damaged heritage sites, reopen learning spaces and support Gaza's journalists, against the $116.5m it says is needed.

The contest over Palestine's story will outlast this genocide, as it has outlasted every massacre and erasure before it. Walls can be levelled and archives burned; the demand to be remembered, and to do the remembering oneself, does not vanish with them.

The task, for scholars, students and the wider public alike, is to ensure that when Palestinians tell the story of what was done to them, and of who they mean to become, it is recognised, at last, as theirs to tell.

title: Gaza buries the remains of 100 Palestinians, including 62 children
summary:
Gaza buries the remains of 100 Palestinians, including 62 children

Palestinians on Sunday held a mass funeral for 100 people, including 62 children, whose remains were recovered from the rubble of buildings destroyed in Israeli strikes in Gaza City.

The bodies, recovered from the al-Zeitoun neighbourhood, included 55 members of the Malaka family who were killed in an Israeli air strike in November 2023, according to Gaza’s civil defence.

The remaining victims belonged to the Irahem, Qanbour, Balawi and Dahdouh families.

Hundreds of people, including relatives and local residents, gathered outside Imam al-Shafi Mosque in al-Zeitoun for the funeral procession, bidding farewell to their loved ones, who were shrouded in Palestinian flags.

title: Mike Huckabee criticised for accusing Jewish UK foreign secretary of 'Jew hate'
summary:
Mike Huckabee criticised for accusing Jewish UK foreign secretary of 'Jew hate'

Submitted by Imran Mulla on Sun, 09/06/2026 - 13:37
US ambassador to Israel's comments mark latest rhetorical attack on UK over its plans to ban Israeli settlement goods
British foreign secretary Ed Miliband speaks as he meets his Spanish counterpart at the Palacio de Viana in Madrid on 29 July 2026 (Leon Neal/AFP)
Off

The US ambassador to Israel has been criticised for accusing the British foreign secretary, who is Jewish, of "Jew hate" over his criticism of Israel's actions in Gaza.

British foreign secretary Ed Miliband released a video earlier this week in which he said: “I just came out of this meeting talking about Gaza to people who've been there and are there on the ground, and frankly it was horrific what is unfolding.”

He asserted that “we as a UK government, as the prime minister has said, have got to act and act more decisively than we have”.

In response, the official X account of Israel's foreign ministry attacked Miliband and said, "facts matter less (when making a video for a political audience)" to the British foreign secretary.

Mike Huckabee, the US ambassador to Israel, shared the Israeli foreign ministry's post and remarked: "The Brits have lost it. The Jew hate of their government knows no boundaries and knows no facts."

Miliband was born in London to Jewish parents who lost family members in the Holocaust.

Numerous commentators online criticised and derided Huckabee for his comments, noting that Miliband is Jewish while Huckabee is not.

Mehdi Hasan, editor-in-chief of Zeteo, posted: "Top US diplomat, Christian evangelical [Huckabee] accuses the Jewish Foreign Secretary of the UK, [Miliband], of 'Jew hate.'"

Hasan remarked: "Funny how the ‘special relationship’ only ever runs one way!"

Shashank Joshi, the Washington bureau chief of The Economist, said: "The way that this administration talks about its closest allies never ceases to astonish. Last week, shaming Canadian soldiers for no apparent reason. This week, accusing the (Jewish) British foreign secretary of 'Jew hate'."

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband described conditions in Gaza as “horrific” after meeting people who had been “on the ground”, citing blocked medicines and children dying while awaiting lifesaving treatment. pic.twitter.com/YwxQI4WLE4

— Middle East Eye (@MiddleEastEye) September 4, 2026

This comes as Miliband prepares to announce a raft of new measures on the occupied West Bank, including a ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements.

In response, Israel has threatened Britain. "If Britain acts against Israel, Israel will act against Britain," foreign minister Gideon Saar warned earlier this week.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has branded the UK the "Islamic Republic of Britain".

His son, Yair Netanyahu, suggested this week that the Falkland Islands belonged to Argentina and not Britain. 

Yair is not a minister, but after his comments, US President Donald Trump indicated that Washington could reconsider its position on British sovereignty over the islands.

On Thursday, Trump even suggested he would not back Britain if Argentina were to invade the Falkland Islands, telling GB News: "Your country was not there to help me" when the US and Israel began their attack on Iran in February.

Argentinian President Javier Milei declared earlier this week that Argentina's national sovereignty had been "violated" and that his country would defend its interests "tooth and nail, no matter who it bothers".

On Friday morning in a national address, Milei threatened sanctions on oil firms that seek to drill around the Falkland Islands, adding that the "winds of change" favoured Argentina's claim to them.

A leaked Pentagon memo from April suggested that Washington could use the Falklands as leverage in negotiations with the UK.

Meanwhile, Miliband is expected to continue preparing sanctions on Israel over its illegal settlements in occupied Palestinian territory.
